column2: Imagine that we walk around the edge of one square, keeping the square on our left. Now add a second square next to it, and walk around that one the same way. On their shared edge, the two walks go in opposite directions. If we add both walks, which edges survive?

The interior seam cancels. Only the outside edge is left. That small cancellation is the visible side of a theorem that connects a change inside a region to an accumulation around its boundary. We will start on a line, build up to surfaces and volumes, and then prove the same pattern in any dimension. At the end, it will explain one of Maxwell's equations.

On a line, a boundary is just a pair of endpoints, with a sign. The boundary of the interval from a to b is b minus a. If we cut the interval in two, the cut point is the positive end of one piece and the negative end of the other. Add the boundaries and that point disappears.

The same cancellation happens with changes of a function. The change across the whole interval is the sum of the changes across its pieces. For a continuously differentiable function, the fundamental theorem of calculus says that adding the derivative over the interval gives the value at b minus the value at a. This is our first Stokes theorem: an integral over an interval equals a signed value on its boundary.

For a region on a plane, the boundary is no longer a pair of points. It is a collection of oriented curves. Give each little tile a counterclockwise boundary. Neighboring tiles traverse their common edge in opposite directions, so the signed contributions from that edge cancel. When we add every tile, the outside edge survives.

What are we adding along those edges? One useful answer is work: along a small step, take the component of a vector field in the direction of that step. Reverse the step and the contribution changes sign. A differential one-form is a general rule for assigning such a signed contribution to a small oriented step. The vector field is a familiar picture; the one-form is the object we integrate.
Here is a one-form simple enough to calculate by hand: omega equals x times d y. Go around the unit square counterclockwise. Which edge contributes anything? Take a moment.

Along the horizontal edges, d y is zero. Along the left edge, x is zero. On the right edge, x is one and y increases by one, so the whole boundary integral is one. The exterior derivative of x d y is d x wedge d y. On the unit square, its integral is the area, also one.
That wedge symbol records oriented area. Reversing the region reverses its induced boundary direction, and both sides change sign. Signs are part of the geometry, not an optional decoration.

Now lift the interior of a disk into a cap, keeping the circular rim fixed. This curved surface sits in three-dimensional space, but it is still two-dimensional: two coordinates locate a point on it. Orient the cap upward. The matching boundary direction is counterclockwise when viewed from above. Your right hand links the two: curl your fingers with the rim and your thumb points along the chosen normal.

Take the vector field whose components are minus y over two, x over two, and zero. Its curl is the constant upward vector. Around the unit circle, the circulation is pi. The upward flux of the curl is also pi, whether we integrate over the flat disk or over this cap. The surfaces share an oriented boundary. We are comparing the flux of the curl, not claiming that every vector field has the same flux through either surface.

Now the object itself is three-dimensional. Its boundary is a two-dimensional surface. Build a solid out of cubes and give each cube outward-facing arrows. On a shared face, the two outward directions oppose each other. Their flux contributions cancel. Only flux through the outside surface remains.

For a concrete example, take the field x, y, z, divided by three. Its divergence is one. The integral of that divergence over a unit ball is the ball's volume, four pi over three. On the unit sphere, the outward component of the field is one third; multiplying by the sphere's area gives the same answer. This is the divergence theorem. It is a volume version of the same boundary relationship, not the same dimensional surface integral we just used for curl.
Here is a trap. Imagine an annulus: a region with a hole in its middle. Its outside edge is a boundary. Is that the whole boundary? Decide which way each edge should be traversed.

The inner edge is a boundary too, with the opposite orientation. Consider the angular one-form, minus y d x plus x d y, divided by x squared plus y squared. On this annulus it is smooth, and its exterior derivative is zero. The outer integral is two pi; the clockwise inner integral is minus two pi. Together they give zero, exactly as the theorem predicts.

If we keep only the counterclockwise loop around the origin, we cannot use a disk containing the origin for this form: the form is undefined there. The missing hypothesis matters. A hole is not a counterexample to Stokes; forgetting a boundary or including a singularity is the mistake.

We have integrated values at points, one-forms along curves, and area-type quantities over surfaces. The dimension tells us what kind of object we integrate. At each point, a k-form is an alternating multilinear rule on k tangent directions. In pictures, it assigns an oriented quantity to a tiny k-dimensional piece: scaling a direction scales the result, and swapping two directions reverses its sign. Its exterior derivative is a k-plus-one-form: it measures the boundary accumulation around a tiny piece one dimension higher.

For a compact oriented smooth n-dimensional manifold with boundary, and a smooth form of degree n minus one, generalized Stokes says: integrate the exterior derivative over the manifold, or integrate the original form over its induced boundary. The answers agree. We will first prove it for a box, then say exactly what extra tools take us to a curved manifold.

Orient an n-dimensional box using the coordinate order one through n. An n-minus-one-form has one term for each missing coordinate. We can write each coefficient beside the wedge of every coordinate differential except the missing one. Choose an alternating sign for each term. That sign is bookkeeping for the orientation of the corresponding faces.

For example, in three dimensions, minus f two d x wedge d z is the same form as plus f two d z wedge d x. Swap the order and the sign flips. The minus sign is not a new physical effect; it keeps the orientation consistent when we put the directions in our chosen order.

Now take the exterior derivative. For each coefficient, its differential includes a contribution in every coordinate direction. What happens when we wedge one of those differentials with the differentials already in the term?

A wedge product vanishes if the same differential appears twice. Every direction already present disappears. Only the derivative in the missing direction survives. Moving that differential into coordinate order produces exactly the sign that cancels the sign we placed in front of the term.

Add the terms and the exterior derivative is the sum of the partial derivatives, multiplied by the oriented n-dimensional volume form. The resemblance to divergence is deliberate. Now we can prove the boundary identity by applying the one-dimensional theorem, one coordinate at a time.

Fix all coordinates except the i-th. Integrating the derivative in that direction gives the coefficient on the upper face minus the coefficient on the lower face. Now integrate those differences over the remaining coordinates. Fubini's theorem lets us perform the integrations in this order for our smooth functions on a bounded box.

The outward-first convention for boundary orientation gives exactly those two signs. Do this for every coordinate and add the results. Every term of the interior integral becomes the matching pair of boundary faces. We have proved generalized Stokes for an oriented box in any number of dimensions. We used the ordinary fundamental theorem, the wedge signs and Fubini; no picture of a four-dimensional object was needed.

What about a curved manifold? The box proof is the local engine, but there are real steps left. We use orientation-preserving coordinate charts. Interior charts look locally like ordinary space; boundary charts look locally like a half-space. We also use a partition of unity: smooth weights, supported inside the charts, that add to one.

Multiply the form by a chart's weight and work in that chart. On an interior chart, compact support makes the opposite contributions vanish. On a boundary chart, the normal-coordinate calculation leaves the boundary-plane term with the outward-first sign. This is again one-variable calculus inside a higher-dimensional integral.
